prompt: What does a tunnel do to the packet it carries?

choices.text: Encrypts it
choices.why: Plain tunnels encrypt nothing; that is what lessons 2 to 4 add.

choices.text: Wraps it inside a new packet
choices.why: Right. Headers and all go inside, and a new IP header goes in front.

choices.text: Rewrites its private addresses to public ones
choices.why: That is NAT. The inner packet keeps 192.168.10.20 and 192.168.20.30.

choices.text: Lays a private cable between the two ends
choices.why: There is no cable: each packet crosses the same routers as everybody else's.

prompt: Which routers read the inner packet's addresses on the way from laptop to till?
hint: Where does the outer header go on and come off?

choices.text: Every router on the path
choices.why: The ISP's router only ever reads the outer header.

choices.text: Only the ISP's
choices.why: The ISP sees 203.0.113.2 and 198.51.100.2 and nothing else it acts on.

choices.text: hq and branch, the two ends
choices.why: Right. Each routes the inner packet into or out of the tunnel.

choices.text: None, the addresses are hidden
choices.why: They are not hidden at all; tcpdump printed them. The ends just route by them.

prompt: How many bytes does an outer IPv4 header add to a tunnelled packet?
Why did the ISP drop the laptop's ping to 192.168.20.30?

choices.text: No route of its own matches a private address
choices.why: Right. It knows three public networks and no 192.168 one.

choices.text: A firewall at the branch blocks ICMP echo requests
choices.why: The packet never reached the branch: it died at the second hop.

choices.text: NAT at hq had been switched off for the test
choices.why: NAT would only have changed the source; the destination is still private.

choices.text: The till was powered off
choices.why: Nothing reached the till to find out.

prompt: Two companies both use 192.168.20.0/24 inside. Why could no internet router ever carry a packet for 192.168.20.30?

choices.text: Private packets are encrypted
choices.why: Nothing about a private address is encrypted.

choices.text: The address is too long to route
choices.why: It is an ordinary 32-bit address.

choices.text: It could not know which one was meant
choices.why: Right. The ranges are private because everybody reuses them.

choices.text: ISPs charge extra for them
choices.why: There is no price at which a route to a reused address makes sense.

prompt: The ISP's routing table listed three public networks and not one ___ network, so the ping to the till died there.
The till's reply arrived with ttl=62 after starting at 64. Which routers took one each?
hint: The ISP never saw the inner packet.

choices.text: branch and the ISP
choices.why: The ISP decremented the outer header's TTL, not the inner one's.

choices.text: branch and hq
choices.why: Right. The two ends route the inner packet; the ISP only forwards the outer one.

choices.text: hq and the ISP
choices.why: Same mistake: the ISP touches only the outer TTL.

choices.text: The till and the laptop
choices.why: Hosts do not decrement the TTL of their own packets.

prompt: What does the route `192.168.20.0/24 via 10.0.0.2` on hq achieve?
hint: 10.0.0.2 is the far end of tun0.

choices.text: It gives the laptop a new address
choices.why: The laptop's address does not change.

choices.text: It tells the ISP where the branch is
choices.why: The ISP never learns about 192.168.20.0/24.

choices.text: Branch traffic goes into tun0
choices.why: Right. Without it the interface exists and nothing goes into it.

choices.text: It opens the tunnel's port on the firewall
choices.why: IP-in-IP has no port at all; it is IP protocol 4.

prompt: tun0 shows POINTOPOINT and NOARP. Why does NOARP make sense for a tunnel?

choices.text: No hardware address exists to ask for
choices.why: Right. ARP maps an IP to a MAC, and a tunnel has neither cable nor MAC.

choices.text: ARP would leak the private addresses to the ISP
choices.why: ARP never leaves a local segment, tunnel or not.

choices.text: ARP is too slow for tunnels
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The far end's MAC is written in the outer header
choices.why: An IP header carries no MAC at all.

prompt: On the GRE capture, the outer packet is 112 bytes and the ping inside it 84. Where do the other 28 come from?

choices.text: 28 bytes of outer IP header, with its options
choices.why: An IPv4 header without options is 20.

choices.text: 20 of GRE header and 8 of padding after it
choices.why: GRE is the smaller of the two, and nothing is padded.

choices.text: A UDP header plus a checksum trailer
choices.why: GRE runs directly on IP, protocol 47, with no UDP.

choices.text: 20 of outer IP, 4 of GRE and 4 of key
choices.why: Right. tcpdump showed GRE's own length as 92, 84 plus 8.

prompt: A colleague proposes using the GRE key as a shared secret, so no stranger can inject packets. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Keys longer than 32 bits are not supported
choices.why: The size is not the problem; its visibility is.

choices.text: It is sent in clear text
choices.why: Right. tcpdump printed key=0x2a on every line, for anyone on the path to copy.

choices.text: A wrong key makes the router reply with an error
choices.why: It replies with nothing; the packet is dropped silently.

choices.text: The key changes every time the tunnel restarts
choices.why: It is configured and stays the same.

prompt: Match each tunnel fact to IP-in-IP or GRE.

pairs.right: IP-in-IP, which has no header of its own
GRE, whose header names the payload

prompt: With the keys set to 42 at hq and 43 at branch, what did the laptop see?
hint: The branch router drops what it does not expect.

choices.text: An error saying the keys differ
choices.why: Nothing tells anybody; that is the trouble with it.

choices.text: Silence: 100% packet loss
choices.why: Right. The packets reach branch and are dropped there, without a word.

choices.text: Replies from the ISP instead of the till
choices.why: The ISP answers nothing inside the tunnel.

choices.text: Only every second ping answered
choices.why: Every packet carries the same wrong key, so every one is dropped.

prompt: An Ethernet link has an MTU of 1500. What is the largest inner packet a GRE tunnel with a key can carry over it, in bytes?
`ping -M do -s 1472` through the IP-in-IP tunnel got `Frag needed and DF set (mtu = 1480)`. Who sent that message?

choices.text: The till, which could not accept 1500 bytes
choices.why: The till never saw it; the packet stopped before the tunnel.

choices.text: The ISP, whose link is too small
choices.why: The ISP's links carry 1500; the refusal came from the tunnel's entrance.

choices.text: hq, whose tunnel carries only 1480
choices.why: Right. It could not forward the packet into tun0 without fragmenting it, and DF forbade that.

choices.text: The laptop's own kernel
choices.why: The laptop's link is 1500, so it sent the packet.

prompt: A branch can open the intranet's login page but every large download hangs with no error. What fits that best?

choices.text: The web server is overloaded
choices.why: An overloaded server is slow for small pages too.

choices.text: DNS returns a different address for large files
choices.why: DNS does not know how large a file is.

choices.text: The tunnel's GRE key does not match at the branch
choices.why: A wrong key would stop the login page too.

choices.text: Big packets die in the tunnel, unannounced
choices.why: Right. A PMTU black hole; lesson 21 finds one.

prompt: After the refusal, `ip route get` showed the laptop remembering the smaller size: `cache expires 599sec mtu ___`.
Capturing GRE on the ISP's router with `tcpdump -A`, what could be read?

choices.text: Only the outer addresses of the two routers
choices.why: The inner addresses and the payload were printed too.

choices.text: The addresses, but not the page that came back
choices.why: `served by files` is the page.

choices.text: Everything: addresses, request and page
choices.why: Right. A plain tunnel encrypts nothing.

choices.text: Nothing, GRE hides the payload
choices.why: GRE hides nothing.

prompt: Which of these does a plain GRE tunnel NOT provide? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Confidentiality of the payload
choices.why: Right: tcpdump read the page.

choices.text: Proof that a packet came from the other office
choices.why: Right: anybody with the outer addresses and the printed key would be accepted.

choices.text: Delivery of private addresses between the offices
choices.why: That it does provide; it is the one thing it is for.

choices.text: Detection of a packet changed on the way
choices.why: Right: nothing checks integrity.

prompt: Put the steps of a packet from laptop to till through the tunnel in order.
items: The laptop sends to 192.168.20.30 via its gateway
hq's route sends it into tun0
hq puts an outer header from 203.0.113.2 to 198.51.100.2
The ISP forwards it by the outer header
branch takes the outer header off and delivers it
trap: The ISP only ever acts on the outer header, which hq adds before it leaves.

prompt: A GRE tunnel between two offices works, and the security team asks for it to be made safe to cross the internet. What is the smallest change that does it?

choices.text: Change the key to a long random number
choices.why: The key is still printed in clear text on every packet.

choices.text: Move the tunnel to IP-in-IP
choices.why: IP-in-IP encrypts no more than GRE does.

choices.text: Protect the GRE traffic with IPsec
choices.why: Right. Encryption and authentication around the tunnel.

choices.text: Lower the tunnel's MTU
choices.why: That changes the size, not who can read it.

prompt: A voice call sends 160-byte packets through a GRE tunnel with a key. Why does the tunnel's overhead matter more here than for a file transfer?
hint: The same 28 bytes, on a smaller packet.

choices.text: The same 28 bytes are a much larger share of a small packet
choices.why: Right. Under 2% on 1500 bytes, far more on 160.

choices.text: Voice packets must be fragmented inside a tunnel
choices.why: They are far below any MTU.

choices.text: GRE adds more header to UDP than it does to TCP
choices.why: GRE adds the same whatever is inside.

choices.text: A tunnel reorders small packets
choices.why: Nothing in GRE reorders anything.
